sections.html:
Three states meet near Dubuque County, which borders the Mississippi in Iowa's far east. The city of Dubuque is the seat and the biggest place, and the whole county held 99,266 people in 2020, ninth highest in Iowa. After the city come Asbury (5,943), Dyersville (4,477), Cascade (2,386), Epworth (2,023), Peosta (1,908) and Farley (1,766).

Hills and woods mark the east, farmland the west. Whether your house is on a bluff street or a farm near Cascade, the same courthouse offices handle your valuation and your bill.

Checks go to the Dubuque County Treasurer. The City of Dubuque states that it neither bills nor collects property tax, and the county forwards the city's portion every month.

Dubuque County property tax contacts
TaskWhere to go
Billing and collectionCounty Treasurer, not the City of Dubuque
Courthouse720 Central Avenue, Dubuque, IA 52001; main line 563-589-1300
Mailing addressPO Box 5001, Dubuque, IA 52004-5001
Hours8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday to Friday
Tax sale biddingOnline at iowataxauction.com

You can book a treasurer appointment online and avoid waiting in line, and the county home page carries a Beacon lookup for property records. One caution: Dubuque also employs a city assessor, so a parcel inside the city may be valued by that office instead of the county. A call to the courthouse with your parcel number clears it up.

The statewide Iowa schedule governs. Your first installment is due September 1 and your second March 1, and each may be paid through the last day of its month.

  • August brings the statements, mailed once the county auditor certifies the levy.
  • Deadlines are September 30 and March 31, sliding to the next business day when they land on a weekend.
  • October is when an unpaid fall half turns delinquent, and April for the spring half.
  • A delinquent installment accrues 1.5 percent monthly, with a one dollar floor.

Iowa bills lag by a year. September and March payments cover the fiscal year that closed the previous June 30, so you may owe for a stretch when the house was yours even if the buyer takes possession before the bill is mailed.

Not getting a statement erases nothing. It is on the owner to see that a bill arrives and gets paid, and a parcel number is enough to make a payment.

Each June, normally on the third Monday, the county auctions parcels with unpaid tax online at iowataxauction.com, and bidders sign up beforehand. One recent publication notice named about 450 real estate parcels and about 130 mobile homes, with amounts due from $6 to $104,077 including penalty and costs.

  • To redeem, you pay 2 percent per month on the sale amount, and a part month is billed as a whole one.
  • After a regular sale, the 90-day notice of right of redemption can issue once one year and nine months run from the sale date.
  • After a public bidder sale, the same notice can issue at nine months.
  • A redemption counts only when the treasurer has it before close of business on the 90th day after service is complete.

An asterisk beside a parcel in the notice means it has been advertised for two years with no buyer. When nobody bids privately, the county bids what is owed. If you hold such a parcel and want to sell, talk with the treasurer before the next June auction.

Assessors start from full market value for homes, and a state rollback percentage trims it to taxable value. The rollback shifts each year, and taxable growth on existing homes statewide is capped at 3 percent. The county reassesses in odd-numbered years, and the Department of Revenue may order an adjustment when a class lands outside a 95 to 105 percent ratio band.

If you think your value is wrong, file a written protest with the Board of Review from April 2 to April 30 of the assessment year. Iowa Code 441.37 gives five grounds:

  • unequal treatment compared with similar property;
  • a value above what the law permits;
  • wrong classification, or a property that should be exempt;
  • an error in the assessment;
  • fraud or misconduct, which must be spelled out.

Ask for a hearing in writing when you file. A written ruling with reasons comes back. Still disagree? The Property Assessment Appeal Board, reachable at 515-725-0338, or district court is the next stop.

Buyers tend to ask about three physical things first: how steep the lot is, whether water reaches it, and how old the systems are. Bluffs shape many Dubuque lots, and low ground by the river and creeks carries flood risk. Aging houses frequently need a new roof, rewiring, foundation work or a sewer line repair before a conventional buyer's inspector is satisfied.

Selling for cash as-is sidesteps that repair list. Even then, check taxes and special assessments with the treasurer before you commit to a date.

Closings usually prorate the year's tax on the statement, either crediting the buyer for the seller's portion or having the seller pay the treasurer directly. If you close from July 1 through December 31, the September installment is yours. Close from January 1 through June 30 and the March installment is yours.

  • Delinquent tax and any sold amounts must be cleared before the title can pass cleanly.
  • A deed for more than $500 carries state transfer tax at 80 cents per $500, or fraction, above $500 (Iowa Code 428A.1).
  • The buyer or seller signs a declaration of value, which goes to the recorder with the deed and then to the assessor, who keeps it for three years.

Since those declarations reach the assessor, your price may later be cited when someone studies values nearby. Keep the settlement statement for your records.

sections.h2: Checklist for an owner about to list
sections.html: Call the courthouse and ask whether your parcel is valued by the county or the city assessor. Request the balance on each half, with interest to your target closing date. Look at the sale notice to see whether the parcel is flagged. Book an appointment online if you would rather not wait. Then hand the figures to the title company so the payoff is ready for the table. If a notice is already out, the delinquent tax, penalty and costs come off your proceeds, and the treasurer can confirm the final number a day or two before closing. Sellers who inherit a house should also ask how long any redemption period still has to run, since that decides how much time there is to act.

faqs.q: Who do I pay property tax to in Dubuque County?
faqs.a: Pay the Dubuque County Treasurer at the courthouse, 720 Central Avenue. The City of Dubuque does not collect it.

faqs.q: What happens if I miss the September 30 payment in Dubuque County?
faqs.a: The first half turns delinquent in October and picks up 1.5 percent a month, never under one dollar. If it stays open, the parcel can be listed for the June sale.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Dubuque County house that is on the tax sale list?
faqs.a: Yes. The overdue tax, penalty and costs are normally paid from your proceeds at closing, and a sold certificate adds 2 percent a month on the sale amount.

faqs.q: When can I protest my Dubuque County assessment?
faqs.a: April 2 through April 30 of the assessment year, in writing, to the Board of Review.

faqs.q: Which payment does a seller owe, September or March?
faqs.a: Close between July 1 and December 31 and you owe September. Close between January 1 and June 30 and you owe March.
